ACX audiobook requirements, and how to check your files before you upload

ACX is the platform that distributes audiobooks to Audible, Amazon and Apple Books. It rejects a submission at quality review when a file breaks one of its published audio rules. The rejection email arrives days later and names the rule, not the file. Here is every file-level rule in one table, with what the free checker does for each.

The rules

RuleWhat ACX asks forPublish Kit
FormatMP3Checked
Bitrate192 kbps or higher, constant bitrate (CBR)Checked. Every frame is read, so a VBR file is caught even without a VBR header
Sample rate44.1 kHzChecked
ChannelsAll files mono, or all files stereo, never mixedChecked across the set
File lengthOne chapter or section per file, at most 120 minutesChecked
CreditsOpening credits and closing credits, each in its own fileFlagged when no file name looks like credits
Retail sampleA separate 1–5 minute sampleFlagged when no file name contains "sample"
RMS loudnessBetween −23 dB and −18 dBMeasured on 16-bit WAV masters
Peak−3 dB or lowerMeasured on 16-bit WAV masters
Noise floor−60 dB RMS or lowerEstimated from the quietest half-second (your room tone) in WAV masters
Room tone0.5–1 s at the head and 1–5 s at the tail of each fileNot checked; listen for it
Cover artSquare, at least 2400 × 2400 px, JPEG, RGBChecked by publish-kit cover cover.jpg --for audiobook

ACX revises its requirements. These are as published when this page was written, so read ACX's own audio submission requirements before you submit.

Why measure loudness on the WAV, not the MP3

Encoding changes peaks slightly, but RMS and noise floor come through MP3 encoding almost unchanged. A WAV master is plain samples, so it can be measured exactly in the browser without decoding. Fix levels on the master, then encode. To measure an MP3 directly, FFmpeg prints RMS and peak with:

ffmpeg -i chapter-01.mp3 -af astats=metadata=0 -f null -

Encoding that passes

ffmpeg -i chapter-01.wav -ar 44100 -ac 1 -codec:a libmp3lame -b:a 192k chapter-01.mp3

-b:a with libmp3lame gives constant bitrate. -q:a gives VBR, the most common reason a file fails the bitrate rule.

From the command line

publish-kit audiobook check audio/*.mp3      # the file rules
publish-kit audiobook check masters/*.wav    # plus loudness
publish-kit audiobook m4b --run              # one chaptered .m4b for direct sale
publish-kit audiobook feed                   # a private podcast-style feed of the chapters

Each command takes --json and exits 1 when a rule fails, so an AI agent or a CI job can loop until the set passes. See the CLI.

PUBLISH KIT · FREE · OPEN SOURCE · NOTHING UPLOADED

Publish your podcast, audiobook or book yourself

Make a podcast RSS feed Apple Podcasts and Spotify accept, turn Markdown into an EPUB for Kindle, Apple Books and Kobo, check audiobook files against ACX, and size a paperback cover. Each tool runs in this page, and the same tools come as a command-line kit an AI agent can drive.

Podcast RSS feedMarkdown → EPUBPaperback spine & coverAudiobook (ACX) checkCLI & AI agents

Podcast RSS feed generator

Fill in the show, drop your episode audio in, and download feed.xml. The page reads each file's size and duration on your device. Upload the audio to any HTTPS host, put the feed next to it, and submit the feed URL to Apple Podcasts Connect and Spotify for Creators.

TitleFileDurationPublish date

  
Episode guids are random UUIDs made once in this page. If you rebuild later, keep the old feed's guids (or use the CLI, which saves them in publish.json). A changed guid makes apps show the episode as new. Check the result with the Podcast Feed Validator.






  
Markdown to EPUB

  
Paste your manuscript in Markdown. Each # Heading starts a new chapter. You get an EPUB 3 file with a cover, a title page and a table of contents, ready for KDP, Apple Books, Kobo, Google Play Books and Draft2Digital. Files from the CLI pass W3C EPUBCheck.

Audiobook file check (ACX / Audible)

  
Choose your chapter files in reading order. Each one is checked against ACX's published requirements: MP3, 192 kbps or higher, constant bitrate, 44.1 kHz, at most 120 minutes, and all mono or all stereo. For 16-bit WAV masters it also measures RMS, peak and noise floor. Files stay on your device.

  
  

  
More detail: ACX audiobook requirements, and how to check your files.






  
The command-line kit, for you or your AI agent

  
The same code as a zero-dependency Node.js CLI. One publish.json per project. Every command takes --json, and plan lists what is still missing and the next command to run, so Claude Code, Cursor or any agent can take a folder of audio or Markdown to a finished feed, EPUB, M4B or print PDF.


git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/duncan-haywood/oss-monorepo
alias publish-kit="node $PWD/oss-monorepo/ventures/publish-kit/cli.mjs"

publish-kit init podcast my-show && cd my-show
publish-kit podcast add ep1.mp3 --title "Pilot" --description "Show notes"
publish-kit plan --json          # what's missing, what to run next
publish-kit podcast build        # dist/feed.xml + dist/index.html, validated

publish-kit init ebook my-book   # chapters/*.md → EPUB, print PDF, cover size
publish-kit ebook build && publish-kit print interior --pdf && publish-kit print cover --pdf dist/my-book-print.pdf

publish-kit init audiobook my-audiobook
publish-kit audiobook check && publish-kit audiobook m4b --run && publish-kit audiobook feed

  
An agent skill file is included (skill/SKILL.md). Source and full docs: ventures/publish-kit on GitHub.





  
Questions

  
How do I make an RSS feed for my podcast without a hosting company?

  
Upload your MP3 files anywhere that serves them over HTTPS (your own site, GitHub Pages, an S3 or R2 bucket), then generate a feed that lists each file's URL, byte size, duration and publish date along with the show's title, description, cover art, category and language. This page does that from the audio files you drop in; the CLI does it from a folder. Host the feed.xml next to the audio and submit its URL to Apple Podcasts Connect and Spotify for Creators.

  
What does ACX require for audiobook files?

  
ACX's published audio submission requirements: each file is one chapter or section and no longer than 120 minutes; MP3 at 192 kbps or higher, constant bitrate, 44.1 kHz; all files mono or all stereo; RMS between -23 and -18 dB, peaks at or below -3 dB, and a noise floor at or below -60 dB RMS; opening and closing credits and a 1 to 5 minute retail sample as separate files; and a square cover of at least 2400 by 2400 pixels. Publish Kit checks the file-level rules and measures loudness on WAV masters.

  
How wide is the spine of my KDP paperback?

  
KDP multiplies the page count by a per-page paper thickness: 0.002252 inches for white paper and 0.0025 inches for cream. A 300-page book on white paper has a 0.676 inch spine, and a 6 by 9 inch book's full cover is then 12.926 by 9.25 inches including 0.125 inch bleed on each edge.

  
Can an AI agent publish my podcast or book with this?

  
Yes. The CLI keeps everything in one publish.json, every command accepts --json, and publish-kit plan returns what is still missing and the next command to run, so an agent such as Claude Code can loop until the project is ready. It never uploads or submits anything itself: you or your agent upload the files and submit the feed, under your own accounts.
